Challah

Made in the Magimix 5200XL — the machine does the mixing and the 10-minute knead in about 1 minute.

Makes1 plaited loaf · 18–20 slices Hands-on≈ 20 min Rising1 hr + 40 min Bake25–30 min · 200C / 180C fan / gas 6

Ingredients

Magimix setup: main 3.6L bowl + dough blade (the short blunt metal blade). 500g flour is comfortably within the 5200XL's dough capacity.
Golden rule: knead in short bursts and stop once smooth — the blade works fast, and over-running heats the dough.
Friday shortcut: steps 1–4 take about 15 minutes. Do them in the morning, let the first rise happen slowly in the fridge all day, then plait, prove and bake before dinner.

Method

  1. Wake the yeastStir the yeast and a pinch of the sugar into 2 tbsp lukewarm water. Leave about 10 minutes until foamy.
  2. Dry mixFit the dough blade. Tip the flour, remaining sugar and salt into the bowl and pulse 2–3 times to combine.
  3. Bring it togetherAdd half the beaten egg, the foamy yeast mixture and the oil. Run the motor and pour 200ml lukewarm water steadily through the feed tube. Within 20–30 seconds the dough should gather into a ball that rides around on the blade. Still floury? Water 1 tbsp at a time with short pulses. Sticky and smearing? Flour 1 tbsp at a time. Moist but not soggy.
  4. Machine kneadOnce the ball forms, keep the motor running a further 45–60 seconds — this replaces the 10-minute hand knead. Done when smooth and it springs back from a gentle poke. Slightly warm is normal.
  5. First riseTurn out, give it 2–3 turns by hand on a lightly floured surface and shape into a tight ball. Roll around a lightly oiled bowl to coat, cover with a tea towel, and leave somewhere warm about 1 hour, until doubled.
  6. PlaitLine a baking sheet with parchment. Divide into 3 equal pieces (weigh them) and roll each into a 25cm rope, slightly tapered at the ends. Don't over-flour — slightly tacky ropes grip each other, so the plait won't split. Pinch together at the top, plait to the bottom, tuck both ends under. Lift onto the sheet.
  7. Second riseCover loosely and leave until puffy and billowy, about 40 minutes. Meanwhile heat the oven to 200C / 180C fan / gas 6.
  8. Glaze & bakeBrush the reserved beaten egg all over, into every crevice; scatter the seeds if using. Bake on the middle shelf 25–30 minutes until deep golden and hollow-sounding when tapped underneath. Check at 15 minutes — tent with foil if darkening fast. Cool on a wire rack.

House rules — the challah & babka doughs

  • Dough blade, main 3.6L bowl. Comfortable up to ~1kg of dough (500g flour is fine). Yeast and salt on opposite sides; pulse the dry mix 2–3×.
  • Liquids through the feed tube, motor running — a ball rides the blade in 20–30s. Floury → water 1 tbsp at a time; smearing → flour 1 tbsp at a time.
  • 45–60 seconds replaces the 10-minute knead. Short bursts, always — the blade heats dough fast. Stop at smooth and springy.
  • Butter goes in via the feed tube, a few soft cubes at a time — then chill butter-rich doughs 30 min before rolling.
  • Our oven is no-fan and runs cool. Trust the probe, not the clock: bread is done at 90–93C in the centre. Tent with foil if the top darkens early.
  • Overnight fridge proof is the house default — knead in the evening, shape and bake in the morning.
  • Yeast comes in 7g sachets. Recipes calling for 5g: the full sachet is fine — prove by size, not the clock.

Adapted for the Magimix 5200XL from BBC Good Food's challah (bbcgoodfood.com/recipes/challah) · photo: our own bake, Aug 2026 · The Household

Sweet Challah

The sweeter version — more sugar, a changed machine method, gentler oven.

Makes1 plaited loaf · 18–20 slices Hands-on≈ 20 min Rising1 hr + 40 min (a little longer) Bake50–60 min · 180C no fan (our oven)

Ingredients

Magimix setup: main 3.6L bowl + dough blade. This dough weighs ≈970g — right at the 5200XL's ~1kg ceiling, so it is the heaviest thing we ask the machine to do.
⚠️ Why this one is not just "challah with more sugar": at 110g sugar to 500g flour (22%) this is a brioche-class dough. Sugar pulls in water and gets in the way of gluten, so the dough runs slack and sticky, never cleanly rides the blade, and can load the motor until it cuts out. Hence: less water up front, sugar added late, short bursts. The extra sugar also slows the yeast — each rise takes 15–20 min longer.
Never fix smearing with flour here. The dough is already at capacity; added flour makes the load worse. Use a short rest instead, or split the batch in two and run it in halves.
If the machine stops on its own: that is the thermal cut-out protecting the motor, not damage. Unplug, leave it 30 minutes to cool. The dough is fine — fold it a few times by hand and carry on, or go straight to the fridge.
Overnight proof (tried & loved): after the machine knead, cover the oiled bowl and refrigerate. Next morning, plait it cold, prove 60–90 min at room temp, glaze and bake.

Method

  1. Wake the yeastStir the yeast and a pinch of the sugar into 2 tbsp lukewarm water. Leave about 10 minutes until foamy.
  2. Dry mixFit the dough blade. Tip in the flour and salt and pulse 2–3 times. The sugar stays out for now — it goes in at step 5.
  3. Bring it togetherAdd half the beaten egg, the foamy yeast mixture and the oil. Run the motor and pour in only ~170ml of the 200ml through the feed tube — keep the last 30ml back. (The yeast slurry is water too, so ~200ml reaches the dough either way.) A ball should gather in 20–30 seconds. Still floury after that? Add the reserved water a tablespoon at a time.
  4. Rest 20 minutesMotor off, lid on, walk away. The flour hydrates and gluten starts forming before the sugar can interfere — this is the single change that stops the dough going to paste.
  5. Now the sugarAdd the 110g sugar in two or three goes, pulsing 10–15 seconds between each. It will look wet and slack as the sugar dissolves — that is expected. Do not chase it with flour.
  6. Machine knead — short bursts10–15 seconds at a time, 45–60 seconds in total, pausing between bursts so neither motor nor dough overheats. Stop at smooth and springy. Going in the fridge overnight? Stop as soon as it comes together — the cold rest does the rest of the work for you.
  7. First riseTurn out, shape into a tight ball, roll around a lightly oiled bowl to coat. Cover and leave somewhere warm about 1 hour, until doubled — sweet dough may want a little longer.
  8. PlaitDivide into 3 equal pieces, roll each into a 25cm rope with tapered ends. Slightly tacky ropes grip — don't over-flour. Plait, tuck the ends under, lift onto a parchment-lined sheet.
  9. Second riseCover loosely and leave until puffy and billowy — about 40 minutes warm, or 60–90 minutes if the dough came out of the fridge. Meanwhile heat the oven to 180C, no fan. Use the poke test, not the clock: press a floured finger 1cm into the dough — springs straight back = not ready; springs back slowly leaving a faint dent = bake now; dent stays put or the dough sighs and sinks = over-proved. Over-proved plaits lose their definition, tear at the seams and bake flat and yeasty; if you get there, knock it back, re-plait and prove again short.
  10. Glaze & bakeBrush with the reserved egg, scatter seeds if using. Bake on the middle shelf 50–60 minutes (timed for our no-fan oven) until deep golden and hollow-sounding underneath — or 91–93C on a probe in the centre. The extra sugar browns fast: check at 20 minutes and tent with foil as soon as the top looks golden. Cool on a wire rack.

House rules — the challah & babka doughs

  • Dough blade, main 3.6L bowl. Comfortable up to ~1kg of dough (500g flour is fine). Yeast and salt on opposite sides; pulse the dry mix 2–3×.
  • Liquids through the feed tube, motor running — a ball rides the blade in 20–30s. Floury → water 1 tbsp at a time; smearing → flour 1 tbsp at a time.
  • 45–60 seconds replaces the 10-minute knead. Short bursts, always — the blade heats dough fast. Stop at smooth and springy.
  • Butter goes in via the feed tube, a few soft cubes at a time — then chill butter-rich doughs 30 min before rolling.
  • Our oven is no-fan and runs cool. Trust the probe, not the clock: bread is done at 90–93C in the centre. Tent with foil if the top darkens early.
  • Overnight fridge proof is the house default — knead in the evening, shape and bake in the morning.
  • Yeast comes in 7g sachets. Recipes calling for 5g: the full sachet is fine — prove by size, not the clock.

Adapted for the Magimix 5200XL from BBC Good Food's challah (bbcgoodfood.com/recipes/challah) · photo: our own bake · The Household

Chocolate Babka

Paul Hollywood's babka, rebuilt for the Magimix 5200XL — nut-free — the machine makes the dough and works in the butter.

Makes1 loaf · 900g tin Hands-on≈ 30 min Chill30 min Prove≈ 2 hr Bake40–45 min · no fan

Ingredients

Dough
Filling
Syrup
Magimix setup: dough blade in the main bowl (≈540g of dough — easily within capacity).
Why the chill: the blade works the dough warm and this one is rich with butter — 30 min in the fridge firms it so the rolling and twisting stay neat.
Overnight option: prove the shaped loaf in its tin in the fridge overnight, then bake from cold in the morning — add 5–10 min and trust the skewer, not the clock.

Method

  1. Make the fillingGently melt the butter, sugar and chocolate in a small pan. Off the heat, stir in the cocoa. Leave to cool until thick and spreadable.
  2. Dry mixFit the dough blade. Add the flour, sugar, yeast and salt (yeast and salt on opposite sides) and pulse 2–3 times.
  3. DoughAdd the beaten eggs and milk and run about 30 seconds, until a soft dough gathers on the blade.
  4. Butter inWith the motor running, drop the butter cubes through the feed tube a few at a time. Run a further 45–60 seconds until smooth, silky and shiny — soft and slightly sticky is exactly right. This replaces the whole stand-mixer knead.
  5. ChillScrape into a bowl, cover, and refrigerate 30 minutes to firm up for rolling.
  6. Fill, roll & twistGrease and line a 900g loaf tin. Roll the dough to a 40 × 30cm rectangle. Spread the filling leaving a 1cm border and roll up tightly from a long edge. Trim the ends, then slice the log in half lengthwise. Cut (stripy) sides up, twist the two halves over each other, pinch the ends, lift into the tin cut-sides up.
  7. ProveCover loosely and leave at room temperature about 2 hours, until doubled and risen to the top of the tin.
  8. BakeHeat the oven to 190C, no fan. Bake 15 minutes, then turn down to 170C for another 25–30 minutes, until a skewer into the centre comes out with no wet dough (chocolate is fine). Our oven runs cool — expect the top end, and give it 10 extra minutes if the skewer says so. Tent with foil if the top darkens early.
  9. SyrupWhile it bakes, boil the sugar and water, then simmer 5 minutes. Brush all of the syrup over the hot babka in its tin — it looks like too much; it isn't. Cool completely before slicing.

House rules — the challah & babka doughs

  • Dough blade, main 3.6L bowl. Comfortable up to ~1kg of dough (500g flour is fine). Yeast and salt on opposite sides; pulse the dry mix 2–3×.
  • Liquids through the feed tube, motor running — a ball rides the blade in 20–30s. Floury → water 1 tbsp at a time; smearing → flour 1 tbsp at a time.
  • 45–60 seconds replaces the 10-minute knead. Short bursts, always — the blade heats dough fast. Stop at smooth and springy.
  • Butter goes in via the feed tube, a few soft cubes at a time — then chill butter-rich doughs 30 min before rolling.
  • Our oven is no-fan and runs cool. Trust the probe, not the clock: bread is done at 90–93C in the centre. Tent with foil if the top darkens early.
  • Overnight fridge proof is the house default — knead in the evening, shape and bake in the morning.
  • Yeast comes in 7g sachets. Recipes calling for 5g: the full sachet is fine — prove by size, not the clock.

Adapted for the Magimix 5200XL from Paul Hollywood's Chocolate Babka (thegreatbritishbakeoff.co.uk) · The Household

Next-Level Chocolate Babka

BBC Good Food's babka, rebuilt for the Magimix 5200XL — dough in the main bowl, filling in the mini bowl, and an overnight rise that fits the routine. Contains almonds.

Serves8 · 900g tin Hands-on≈ 30 min Chillovernight Prove2–3 hr Bake≈45 min · 180C no fan · 90C inside

Ingredients

Dough
Filling
Syrup
Magimix setup: dough blade in the main bowl for the dough; mini bowl + mini blade for the filling paste. No stand mixer needed.
The chill is the recipe: this dough is designed to rest in the fridge overnight — cold, firm dough is what gives the sharp chocolate layers.
Same-day fallback: no overnight? Rise 2 hrs at room temp, then chill at least 1 hr — never roll it warm.

Method

  1. Dry mixFit the dough blade. Add the flour, cinnamon (if using), sugar, yeast and salt (yeast and salt on opposite sides) and pulse 2–3 times.
  2. DoughAdd the milk and eggs and run 30–45 seconds until a smooth, soft dough forms on the blade. Rest it in the bowl, lid on, for 10 minutes — this replaces the long mixer knead.
  3. Butter inWith the motor running, drop the butter cubes through the feed tube a few at a time, then run 45–60 seconds until silky and shiny. Soft and sticky is correct.
  4. Overnight chillScrape into a buttered bowl, cover, and refrigerate overnight, until nearly doubled.
  5. Filling (mini bowl)Melt the chocolate (bain-marie, or 10-second microwave bursts) and let it cool. In the mini bowl, blitz the butter, sugar and ground almonds; add the cocoa, melted chocolate and a pinch of sea salt and pulse to a spreadable paste.
  6. Fill & rollRoll the cold dough on a floured surface to a 30 × 40cm rectangle, long edge towards you. Spread the filling to a thin border, scatter the flaked almonds, and roll away from you into a tight log. If there's fridge space, chill the log 1 hour, seam-side down — it sharpens the layers.
  7. TwistButter a 900g loaf tin, line with a parchment strip overhanging both ends. Cut the log in half lengthwise with a serrated knife, lay the pieces parallel, and plait to about 8 twists. Lift into the tin, tuck the ends under, fatten the plait to fit.
  8. ProveCover with a tea towel and leave at room temperature 2–3 hours, until risen by about half.
  9. BakeHeat the oven to 180C, no fan. Bake about 45 minutes until dark golden — done at 90C on a probe in the middle. Our oven runs cool: trust the probe, not the clock, and tent with foil if the top darkens early.
  10. SyrupBoil the sugar with 4 tbsp water until dissolved. Brush over the hot babka in stages, letting each coat soak in, until it's all gone. Cool fully before slicing. Best on the day; keeps 2 days airtight.

House rules — the challah & babka doughs

  • Dough blade, main 3.6L bowl. Comfortable up to ~1kg of dough (500g flour is fine). Yeast and salt on opposite sides; pulse the dry mix 2–3×.
  • Liquids through the feed tube, motor running — a ball rides the blade in 20–30s. Floury → water 1 tbsp at a time; smearing → flour 1 tbsp at a time.
  • 45–60 seconds replaces the 10-minute knead. Short bursts, always — the blade heats dough fast. Stop at smooth and springy.
  • Butter goes in via the feed tube, a few soft cubes at a time — then chill butter-rich doughs 30 min before rolling.
  • Our oven is no-fan and runs cool. Trust the probe, not the clock: bread is done at 90–93C in the centre. Tent with foil if the top darkens early.
  • Overnight fridge proof is the house default — knead in the evening, shape and bake in the morning.
  • Yeast comes in 7g sachets. Recipes calling for 5g: the full sachet is fine — prove by size, not the clock.

Adapted for the Magimix 5200XL from BBC Good Food's Next-level chocolate babka (bbcgoodfood.com/recipes/next-level-chocolate-babka) · The Household

Biscuit Cake

Esti Rotem's nostalgic no-bake classic from mako Food — let the kids make it, almost no help needed. Biscuits, a creamy vanilla filling, and chocolate on top.

Tin30 × 18cm rectangular Hands-on≈ 20 min Chill3 hr minimum Ovennone — no-bake

Ingredients

Base
Filling
Topping
UK shopping (house note — this is an Israeli recipe): biscuits = petit beurre or Rich Tea. Cream: the sweet cream this recipe uses in Israel is 32% fat — UK whipping cream (~35%) is the match; double cream (48%) whips too heavy, single (18%) won't whip. White cheese (gvina levana, ~5%): use Fage Total 5% Greek yogurt (weigh out 500g) or quark. Pudding = the powdered instant vanilla mix (Osem/Jell-O) — kosher shops, American aisles or Amazon, not a supermarket staple.
Why this whipping order (mako editors): the original whips everything together — most get a great result, some find it too loose. Whipping the cream, pudding, milk and sugar first, then adding the cheese, keeps it stable.
Keeps: in the fridge. Freezing not recommended.

Method

  1. Whip the creamWhip the whipping cream with the pudding mix, milk and sugar to a stable whipped cream. Add the cheese and lemon zest and whip only until incorporated.
  2. Dip & layerIn a deep plate, mix the ½ cup milk with the vanilla and the shot of coffee. Dip each biscuit — a quick, short dunk — and lay in a 30 × 18cm rectangular tin to form a layer of biscuits.
  3. FillGently spread half the cream over the biscuits. Cover with a second layer of dipped biscuits. Spread the rest of the cream and cover with a third biscuit layer.
  4. Chocolate top & chillGrate 70% dark chocolate generously over the top — our way. (The original melts 100g chocolate with 120ml cream in 30-second microwave bursts until glossy, and pours it over.) Refrigerate at least 3 hours.

Translated for The Household from Esti Rotem's biscuit cake on mako Food (mako.co.il, first published 2012) · rated 4.6 by 11,500+ home cooks

Banana Oatmeal Pancakes

Monique Volz's blender pancakes from Ambitious Kitchen — the whole batter is blitzed smooth, no flour, naturally sweetened by ripe bananas. Contains almond milk.

Makes9 pancakes · serves 3 Prep10 min Cook10 min Ovennone — pan or griddle

Ingredients

No blender? (house note): the Magimix main bowl with the standard metal blade should handle this batter — blitz until the oats disappear and it pours smoothly.
Freezer-friendly: freeze the cooked pancakes flat on a tray for 30 minutes so they don't stick together, then bag them up — keeps up to 3 months.

Method

  1. BlendAdd all the ingredients to a blender and blend on high until completely smooth, about 30 seconds to 1 minute. Let the batter sit in the blender while the pan heats up.
  2. First sideLightly coat a griddle or pan with coconut oil, vegan butter or olive oil over medium heat. Once hot, add ⅓ cup of batter per pancake and cook 2–4 minutes, until they slightly puff up and a few bubbles show along the edges.
  3. FlipFlip and cook until golden on the underside. Browning too fast? Lower the heat — start medium, drop to medium-low. A smoking pan is a too-hot pan.
  4. RepeatWipe the pan clean and repeat with more oil and the remaining batter. Makes 9 pancakes — serves 3, three each.

From Monique Volz's Healthy Banana Oatmeal Pancakes (ambitiouskitchen.com/banana-oatmeal-pancakes) · The Household

Crazy Chocolate Cake

Daniel Amit's chocolate cake from foody — insanely moist, rich, and made for birthdays. The skewer comes out damp on purpose.

Tin31 × 22cm rectangular Hands-on≈ 20 min Bake40–45 min · see oven note Serves12

Ingredients

Cake
Ganache
UK shopping (house note — this is an Israeli recipe): Shokolit = sweetened chocolate drink powder — use drinking chocolate (e.g. Cadbury), NOT pure cocoa. This recipe names 38% sweet cream — UK whipping cream (~35%) is the nearest; double cream also works in the ganache.
Oven (house note): the original bakes at 160C fan. Ours is no-fan and runs cool — use 180C conventional and trust the skewer: it should come out moist, not clean.

Method

  1. WhiskWhisk the eggs and sugar, by hand or in a mixer.
  2. Build the batterGradually add the rest — the oil, chocolate drink powder, flour, instant coffee and salt.
  3. Melt & foldIn a separate pan, melt the cream with the dark and milk chocolate. Once melted, add to the batter and mix until no lumps remain.
  4. BakePour into a greased 31 × 22cm tin and bake in the preheated oven 40–45 minutes (see the oven note). Take it out when a skewer comes out moist.
  5. GanacheMelt the cream with the milk and dark chocolate in a pan over low heat.
  6. Pour & sprinkleWhile the cake is still warm, cut it in the tin, pour the ganache all over, let it cool a little, and finish with colourful sprinkles.

Translated for The Household from Daniel Amit's chocolate cake (danielamit.foody.co.il) · 1M views, rated 4/5 by 933 home cooks · photo: our own bake

Double Chocolate & Mascarpone Traybake

Benjamina Ebuehi's one-bowl crowd cake from Guardian Feast — velvety crumb, milk-chocolate mascarpone frosting. Family-tested: "Very nice cake!"

Tin23 × 33cm, lined with overhang Prep20 min Cook40 min Serves16

Ingredients

Cake
Frosting
Oven (house note): the recipe's 180C conventional is exactly our no-fan setting — but ours runs cool, so expect the top of the 35–40 min window and trust the skewer.

Method

  1. Tin & ovenHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan) / gas 4. Grease a 23 × 33cm baking tin, then line with greaseproof paper, leaving enough overhang to lift the cake out once baked.
  2. MeltPut the chocolate and butter in a heatproof bowl and melt in short microwave bursts, or over a pan of simmering water. Set aside to cool.
  3. One-bowl batterIn a large bowl, mix the flour, cocoa, sugar, baking powder, bicarb and salt. Make a well in the centre, pour in the eggs, oil, milk and cooled chocolate-butter mix, and whisk to a thick, smooth batter. Pour in 150ml hot water and mix again until well combined.
  4. BakePour into the prepared tin and bake 35–40 minutes, until a skewer inserted into the middle comes out clean. Take out and leave to cool.
  5. Frosting basePut the chocolate, butter, cocoa, half the cream and the salt in a small saucepan and heat very gently until just melted.
  6. Whisk in mascarponePut the mascarpone in a bowl, pour the chocolate mixture over, and whisk well to combine. Add the rest of the cream, mix until smooth, then leave to cool and thicken to a spreadable consistency.
  7. Frost & finishSpread the frosting all over the top and sides, top with shaved chocolate, then cut into slices and serve.

From Benjamina Ebuehi's double chocolate and mascarpone traybake — Guardian Feast, The Sweet Spot (theguardian.com, 3 May 2024) · clipped from the paper & family-approved
